To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the brain uses two different coding schemes for spatial memory, that the two coding schemes are used in different situations, and that the coding schemes interact to produce a unified representation of space.

(1) there is a complex interplay between allocentric and egocentric coding, (2) this interplay is not well captured by a discrete distinction between egocentric/egocentric coding and (3) the complex interplay can be understood in the context of embodied cognition.
(i) the hippocampal system represents space in a manner that is both allocentric and egocentric and (ii) the hippocampally-mediated representation of space is embodied.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the complex interplay between the body and space, and between egocentricity and allocentricity, in spatial representation and behavior.
the neural basis of spatial representation.
the neural basis of three-dimensional spatial representations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the egocentric and the allocentric representations are complementary and interdependent.
egocentric and egocentric coding are not distinct but are instead interwoven in a complex way.
the brain represents three-dimensional space in an embodied way that integrates allocentric and egocentric coding.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the brain uses multiple codes for spatial representation, including egocentric, allocentric, and object-centered coding.
the egocentric-allocentric distinction is not as clear as we thought, and that the interplay between the two is more complex and interesting than previously appreciated.
egocentric and alloctetric coding are not discrete but are instead two aspects of a more general, integrated, and embodied system of spatial representation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the egocentric and the allocentric are better understood as a complex interplay, rather than as discrete and independent codes.
the brain’s spatial representations are not as discrete as Jeffery et al.’s proposal suggests, and that a complex interaction between egocentricity and allocentricity is required.
egocentric coding is not the same as coding in the body-centered reference frame.
